[PAPER_0050, relevance_score=0.378] Our first aim was to verify the validity of the EV index by replicating Vine et al.'s (2020) initial findings linking EV to essential psycholinguistic, demographic, and personality variables. Next, we tested two competing hypotheses examining the EV-ED relationship. The lexical facilitation hypothesis suggests larger negative and positive EV will be associated with higher negative and positive ED, respectively. Alternatively, the emotion concision hypothesis suggests larger negative and positive EVs will be associated with lower negative and positive ED, respectively.

[PAPER_0104, relevance_score=0.296] Exploratory Analyses

An alternative model that could feasibly explain the EV-ED relationship is that low NED increases risk for depression, which in turn leaves adolescents more likely to discuss a wider range of stressors, leading to higher EV (effectively, depression mediating the relationship between NED and NEV).

[PAPER_0107, relevance_score=0.356] Because we proposed competing hypothesis predicting opposite relationships between EV and ED, as a post hoc exploratory (nonpreregistered) test, we examined whether there may be an inverted U-shaped relationship between these two variables, reflecting heterogeneity in the ED-EV relationship, such that low ED is observed both when EV is high (in line with the emotion concision model) and when EV is low (in line with lexical facilitation). Both linear and quadratic terms of EV were entered into a regression model predicting ED.

[PAPER_0141, relevance_score=0.315] Note that the naming of the models deviates from those used in the preregistration. This is to increase clarity and prevent confusion with redundant emotional constructs.
items.paper_content_summary: The paper describes a replication aim, competing positive and negative EV–ED hypotheses, and predicts that depression is positively associated with negative EV and negatively associated with positive EV. It also presents post hoc possibilities involving depression-mediated EV–ED relationships and an inverted-U relationship [PAPER_0050] [PAPER_0051] [PAPER_0104] [PAPER_0107].

[PREREG_0006, relevance_score=0.376] These transcripts are significantly longer than written responses in prior experimental work. The present study also utilizes multiple measures of depression and ED derived from EMA data. These strengths leave us well positioned to examine EVs in the context of spoken language in a rich developmental sample.

q2: H1: Replicating previous work examining EVs (Vine et al., 2020), we anticipate that larger negative EVs will be negatively associated with the following text-derived variables: positive emotional tone, we-words and leisure words.

[PREREG_0007, relevance_score=0.376] We expect negative EVs to be positively associated with the following text-derived variables: cognitive processing, negative emotional tone, general vocabulary size, illness words, I-words, affiliation words and achievement words. We anticipate that negative EVs will be positively associated with self-reported neuroticism, and that negative EVs will be higher among females.

We anticipate that larger positive EVs will be negatively associated with the following text derived variables: cognitive processing & we-words.

[PREREG_0008, relevance_score=0.370] We anticipate that positive EVs will be positively associated with the following text-derived variables: positive emotional tone, general vocabulary size, illness words, affiliation words, achievement words and leisure words. We expect positive EV to be negatively associated with self-reported neuroticism and age.

As a test of robustness, we will also examine these associations when controlling for general vocabulary size and emotional tone.

[PREREG_0009, relevance_score=0.451] H2: We will test two competing hypotheses when examining the association between EVs and ED: 1) The emotion lexicon hypothesis suggests that larger negative and positive EVs will be associated with higher negative and positive ED respectively. 2) The emotion complexity hypothesis suggests that larger negative and positive EVs are associated with lower negative and positive ED.

As a test of robustness, we will also examine these associations when controlling for general vocabulary size and emotional tone.

[PREREG_0010, relevance_score=0.352] As a second test of robustness, if either ED variables show significant associations with EV variables, we will control for emotional intensity corresponding to the valence of the ED variable (i.e., controlling for positive emotional intensity if the positive ED is significant, and negative emotional intensity if negative ED is significant).

H3: We hypothesize that more depressive symptoms will be associated with larger negative EVs and lower depressive symptoms with smaller positive EVs. As a test of robustness, we will also examine these associations when controlling for general vocabulary size and emotional tone.

[PREREG_0011, relevance_score=0.398] H4: We hypothesize that more depressive symptoms will be associated with larger negative EVs and lower depressive symptoms with smaller positive EVs, above and beyond the relationship between negative and positive ED and depressive symptoms. As a test of robustness, we will also examine these associations when controlling for general vocabulary size and emotional tone.

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0017, relevance_score=0.276] In the emotional concision hypothesis, we theorized that ED may reflect narrower emotional experiences that are more succinctly labelled, which could result in larger EV being associated with lower ED. A community sample of adolescents (N = 241, ages 14-17, predominantly White) completed interviews, self-report measures, and ecological momentary assessments as part of a larger study conducted between 2014 and 2016. EV was derived using speech samples from transcribed recordings of life stress interviews. In line with the emotion concision hypothesis, EV and ED were inversely related for negative emotions.

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.474] Method

Participants

The present study uses data collected as part of a larger study on adolescent internalizing disorders and emotion processes (Starr, Dienes, et al., 2017).

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.479] A community sample of 241 adolescents (Mage = 15.9 years, SD = 1.09; 53% girls, 46% boys, 1% other gender; 73.9% White, 12.2% Black, 4.1% Asian, 7.1% multiracial, 2.1% other/not reported, 0.4% Native American; 9.1% Hispanic or Latino) was recruited from a midsized metropolitan area of the northeastern United States.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.437] Participants were recruited from multiple sources, including online and community flyers, commercial mailing lists, and ResearchMatch (a national health volunteer registry). The recruitment team made intentional efforts to distribute flyers in socioeconomically diverse areas of the community. Exclusion criteria included lack of fluency in English, evidence of a pervasive developmental disorder, prior diagnosis of bipolar or psychotic disorder, presence of a major physical or neurological disorder that would impair questionnaire/interview completion, and prior participation of another household member.

[PAPER_0060, relevance_score=0.336] In this way, transcribed LSIs create an opportunity to examine active or spontaneous EV in the context of recalling emotionally salient experiences. Prior analyses support transcribed LSIs as a rich source of psycholinguistic data (Sheinbaum et al., 2024).

Audio recordings of the LSI were automatically transcribed using NVivo (Edhlund & McDougall, 2019) and hand-checked using recordings for accuracy. Interviewer speech was removed to isolate participant speech.

[PAPER_0078, relevance_score=0.379] Procedure

Participants and their primary caregivers attended an in-person lab session (between December 2014 and October 2016) during which they completed the LSI, K-SADS, and questionnaires, and were given instructions for the completion of daily surveys. Starting the day after the in-person lab session, adolescents were asked to complete surveys four times a day for 7 days on their personal smartphones or a study-provided tablet.

[PAPER_0079, relevance_score=0.333] Surveys schedules were nonrandom to accommodate school hours, at approximately 4-6-hr intervals, with one survey prompt in the morning, two survey prompts midday (lunch and after school) and one survey prompt before bedtime. Participants earned up to $160 total in compensation depending on compliance. EMA completion was monitored daily, and study staff contacted participants to troubleshot technical issues and encourage survey completion as needed.

Secondly, these studies relied on self-reported or text-derived measures of depression.

The present study aims to replicate and extend this work using a rich adolescent dataset. EVs will be harvested from transcripts of UCLA Life Stress Interviews, thereby allowing examination of these constructs in the context of spoken language in reference to emotionally salient topics (DeLap et al., 2022).

[PAPER_0049, relevance_score=0.246] The Present Study

The present study used a multimethod approach to replicate and extend the foundational work in EV in an adolescent sample. EV was derived from transcripts of audiorecorded life stress interviews (LSIs), allowing for examination of these constructs in the context of spoken language in reference to emotionally salient topics. We modeled latent depression using a multi-informant set of assessments to minimize measurement error and derived ED using ambulatory EMA methods (Hill & Updegraff, 2012; Tugade & Fredrickson, 2007).

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.253] Method

Participants

The present study uses data collected as part of a larger study on adolescent internalizing disorders and emotion processes (Starr, Dienes, et al., 2017).

[PAPER_0086, relevance_score=0.289] Results

Preliminary Analyses

Descriptive data and bivariate correlations among major study variables are presented in Table 1, as are partial correlations (which serve as our robustness test and control for general vocabulary sizes and negative and positive emotional tone). Correlations between all study variables, including common Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count indicators, can be found on Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/4j75w/.

[PAPER_0091, relevance_score=0.363] Depression Measurement Model

We estimated a series of preregistered measurement models using multiple depression measures (Depression Anxiety Stress Scale depression subscale, KSADS, BDI somatic symptoms subscale, BDI cognitive affective symptoms subscale, parent- and child-reported emotional problems subscale SDQ) to derive a latent depression factor. For each model, theoretically justified modification indices were incorporated to examine improvement in fit (e.g., correlating the residual variances of the parent- and child-reported SDQ).

[PAPER_0092, relevance_score=0.275] Comparisons between the three preregistered latent depression models can be found on OSF at https://osf.io/4j75w/. The best-fitting and therefore final latent model of depression included the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale, KSADS, both BDI subscales and the child-reported SDQ. In a deviation from the preregistration, we excluded the parent-reported SDQ due to poor local fit across models (.36-42).

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0082, relevance_score=0.412] Mplus uses full information maximum likelihood estimation to estimate missing data on endogenous variables. We first used a preregistered model-comparison approach to develop a latent measurement model of depression using available depression scores. Latent variable modeling of depression allows for a multimethod, multi-informant approach (here, interview and self-report measures), reducing error variance (Bollen, 1989; Kline, 2023). We then ran a series of structural models regressing depression on EV alone and EV and ED together. Model fit criteria were preregistered.

[PAPER_0083, relevance_score=0.400] Model fit criteria were preregistered. Acceptable model fit included a nonsignificant χ2 likelihood ratio test, comparative fit index (CFI) ≥.90 and a root-mean-square error of approximation (RMSEA) below ≤.10 (Brown, 2015).

Consistent with prior work on EV (Vine et al., 2020), robustness analyses controlling for general vocabulary size and both positive and negative emotional tone were performed. Robustness tests of bivariate associations took the form of multiple regression and are reported as partial correlations.

[PAPER_0084, relevance_score=0.429] Structural equation model robustness analyses included these control variables as covariates in the model. For structural models which resulted in significant associations between ED and depression, we ran a nonpreregistered secondary robustness test, omitting the opposing emotional tone (e.g., omitting positive tone as a covariate for NEV). This secondary robustness test was added to account for the possibility that our initial robustness criteria were unnecessarily conservative, given the lack of association between emotional tone and EV of different valences.

[PAPER_0086, relevance_score=0.371] Results

Preliminary Analyses

Descriptive data and bivariate correlations among major study variables are presented in Table 1, as are partial correlations (which serve as our robustness test and control for general vocabulary sizes and negative and positive emotional tone). Correlations between all study variables, including common Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count indicators, can be found on Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/4j75w/.

[PAPER_0091, relevance_score=0.396] Depression Measurement Model

We estimated a series of preregistered measurement models using multiple depression measures (Depression Anxiety Stress Scale depression subscale, KSADS, BDI somatic symptoms subscale, BDI cognitive affective symptoms subscale, parent- and child-reported emotional problems subscale SDQ) to derive a latent depression factor. For each model, theoretically justified modification indices were incorporated to examine improvement in fit (e.g., correlating the residual variances of the parent- and child-reported SDQ).

[PAPER_0092, relevance_score=0.349] Comparisons between the three preregistered latent depression models can be found on OSF at https://osf.io/4j75w/. The best-fitting and therefore final latent model of depression included the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale, KSADS, both BDI subscales and the child-reported SDQ. In a deviation from the preregistration, we excluded the parent-reported SDQ due to poor local fit across models (.36-42).

[PAPER_0098, relevance_score=0.325] Emotion Vocabulary, Emotion Differentiation, and Depression

Next, we tested additional structural models (one each for positive- and negative-valence variables) that examined the unique predictive associations between EV and ED and latent depression, again split by valence.

[PAPER_0105, relevance_score=0.313] Although we lack the multiwave panel data to appropriately test mediation, we tested a post hoc (nonpreregistered) structural model where NED and latent depression simultaneously predicted NEV to determine whether the relationship between NED and NEV persists beyond the possible mediational role of depression. A chi-square test indicated a deviation from perfect fit, χ2(14) = 35.82, p = .001, but other indices were acceptable (RMSEA = .08; CFI = .95).

[PAPER_0107, relevance_score=0.293] Because we proposed competing hypothesis predicting opposite relationships between EV and ED, as a post hoc exploratory (nonpreregistered) test, we examined whether there may be an inverted U-shaped relationship between these two variables, reflecting heterogeneity in the ED-EV relationship, such that low ED is observed both when EV is high (in line with the emotion concision model) and when EV is low (in line with lexical facilitation). Both linear and quadratic terms of EV were entered into a regression model predicting ED.
